title: No-scalpel vasectomy
subtitle: Fix each vas under the skin, divide, seal the lumen and interpose fascia

sources.title: BAUS procedure-specific patient information and consent guidance

indications: A man who has decided on permanent contraception after counselling.
contraindications: Scrotal infection, or a scrotum where the vas cannot be felt (needs a different setting).
preparation: Counselling: permanent, not immediately effective, failure about 1 in 2000 after clearance, chronic scrotal pain in a few, reversal is not guaranteed.
Shave or trim the scrotum if needed.
positioning: Supine, the penis taped up on the abdomen, a warm room so the scrotum is relaxed.
equipment: Ring clamp, sharp dissecting forceps, diathermy needle or fine cautery, absorbable ties or clips, local anaesthetic.
anatomy: Vas deferens (firm cord at the back of the spermatic cord), testicular artery and pampiniform veins, the median raphe.
criticalSafety: Both vasa are divided; the patient knows he is not sterile until a clear semen test.
commonErrors: Dividing a vein or nerve instead of the vas.
Telling the patient he is sterile on the day.
postop: Scrotal support, simple analgesia, rest for 1 to 2 days.
Other contraception until a semen test about 12 weeks later shows no sperm (or rare non-motile sperm per guideline).
Return for a growing swelling or fever.

steps.emphasis: Permanent; not immediate; a later semen test; the failure and pain rates.
Supine, penis taped up onto the abdomen, scrotum relaxed in a warm room.
Clean the scrotum; a fenestrated drape.
Check both ends and the sheath for bleeding before returning the vas.
Short vas segments sent if local policy requires histology.
The small puncture usually needs no stitch; pressure and a dry dressing.
Contraception continues until the semen test is clear; give the test date and pot.

step.vas.fix.title: Three-finger fix of the vas
step.vas.fix.why: Holding the vas firmly under the skin at one spot makes the procedure short and keeps the vessels out of the way.
how: Feel the right vas at the back of the cord and roll it to the front under the median raphe.
Trap it between thumb, index and middle finger (three-finger technique) so it lies just under thin skin.
Confirm it is the vas: firm, cord-like and separate from the softer vessels.
pitfalls: Fixing a vein instead of the vas.

step.vas.local.title: Local anaesthetic block of the vas
step.vas.local.why: A vasal block numbs the vas and its sheath; a skin weal alone is not enough.
how: Raise a skin weal over the fixed vas.
Advance the needle along the vas towards the inguinal ring and inject a few ml into the sheath (or use a no-needle jet injector).

step.vas.deliver.title: Puncture and deliver a loop of vas
step.vas.deliver.why: A small puncture with sharp forceps heals without stitches and causes fewer haematomas than a scalpel incision.
how: Hold the vas in the ring clamp through the skin.
Puncture skin and sheath with one blade of the sharp forceps, spread to open a small hole down to the vas.
Lift a loop of bare vas out of the hole, stripping the sheath off it.
pitfalls: Spreading too widely and tearing vessels.

step.vas.divide.title: Divide, seal and interpose fascia
step.vas.divide.why: Sealing the cut lumen and putting a layer of fascia between the ends gives the lowest failure rate.
how: Divide the vas and remove a short segment if policy requires.
Cauterise the lumen of each end for about 1 cm with a fine needle cautery.
Close the sheath over one end (fascial interposition) with a tie or clip so the ends lie in different planes.
pitfalls: Leaving the two ends lying together without interposition.

step.vas.other-side.title: The other side, same way
step.vas.other-side.why: Both vasa must be divided. The left side is done through the same puncture once the right is returned.
how: Return the right vas and confirm no bleeding.
Fix the left vas under the same puncture and repeat block, delivery and division.
Confirm two divided vasa before finishing.
pitfalls: Dividing the same vas twice and missing the other.
